Where the evidence falls short

Fully met: program completion, faculty preparation, course-level teaching quality, NCLEX-PN performance, and systematic evaluation. Most Student Learning Outcomes are partly met: earlier SPOE ratings reached the benchmark, but the 2025–2026 exit survey did not. Not yet measured: public service, faculty continuing education, scholarly activity, and graduate professional development.

Statistical models: what the data can and cannot tell us

Three ways of looking at AMG's numbers, each answering one plain question. Because AMG has only three to five years of results for most measures, every answer comes with real uncertainty, and the charts show it openly. Use them to think and plan, not as official predictions.

Are results really going up or down over the years?

The solid line is the best straight line through each year's result (the dots). The shaded area shows where the true line could reasonably fall. The vertical bar at the next year shows the range where next year's result could land. The wider the shading and the bar, the less the data can tell us.

Students rated many areas higher in spring 2026 than in fall 2025. Is that a real improvement, or just chance?

Only about 50 to 60 students answered each survey, so some movement is expected by luck alone. Each curve shows the likely range of the true share of satisfied students: the peak is the most likely value, and a narrower curve means more certainty. When the blue spring 2026 curve sits clearly to the right of the orange fall 2025 curve, the improvement is probably real.

Fall 2025Spring 2026

How much each area changed, fall 2025 to spring 2026

Each row is one survey area. The dot is the best estimate of how much it changed from fall 2025 to spring 2026, and the bar shows the likely range. If the whole bar sits to the right of the zero line, the area almost certainly improved. The percentage on the right is the chance the improvement is real. Select a row to see its curves above.

Almost certainly improvedProbably improved (at least an 80% chance)Too close to call

System dynamics: how the pieces feed back on each other over five years

Built on the path model, this simulation adds what a path model can't show: stocks that build up or drain over time (students, faculty, readiness, climate, reputation), flows between them (admissions, graduation, attrition, hiring, turnover), and feedback loops. Starting values come from AMG's 2025–2026 data; the strengths of the connections are planning assumptions, so read the results as "what tends to happen if," not forecasts.

For statisticians: methods, results, and limits

What might the 2026 NCLEX-RN pass rate look like?

The computer imagines 2026 ten thousand times. Each time, it starts from last year's 71%, adds a possible boost from the new review sessions and supports, adds the kind of random ups and downs seen in past years, and then "tests" each student. Each bar shows how often a result came up. Red bars fall short of 80%, orange bars reach 80% but not 85%, and green bars reach 85% or higher. Move the sliders to try different assumptions.

The real number isn't in the documents, so this starts at 183, the number of 2025 RN graduates. Set it to the actual number if known.
How many points the review sessions, BOOT Camp, and ATI remediation might add. The simulation treats this boost as uncertain, not guaranteed.
AMG's PN pass rate has moved up or down by about 6 to 7 points in a typical year.

How might all these factors work together to produce AMG's results?

This is a path model, the kind analyzed with structural equation modeling (SEM). Ovals are broad qualities that can't be measured directly, such as teaching quality. Each is gauged through several survey scores or records. Boxes are results AMG reports directly. Each arrow is a link AMG's documents suggest: "this is expected to affect that." Until student-level data is loaded below, the arrows show expected links only, without measured strengths.The arrows show expected links. Their strengths will be estimated once student-level records are linked, a step already on AMG's schedule.

Can this model be tested with AMG's current data?

Not yet but AMG is close

To measure how strongly each arrow pushes, SEM needs one row of data per student: that student's ATI levels, course grades, advising visits, survey answers, any records errors, and whether they stayed, graduated, passed the NCLEX, and found work within six months. The September 24 documents add a full year of Student Services records and a second graduate survey, but these are still program-wide counts and averages, not per-student records. Averages show where the program stands, not which factors drive which results.

Put numbers on the arrows

Load a spreadsheet with one row per student and the page estimates every arrow it has columns for. Each arrow gets a path coefficient (β, how strongly two things move together, from −1 to 1) and a p-value (how likely a link that strong would appear by pure chance). Your file stays in this browser: nothing is uploaded or saved.

No data loaded. The diagram shows the expected links only.

What columns should the file have?

Use these column names in the first row. Any column can be missing; arrows that need it are simply left unestimated. Yes/No and Pass/Fail are read as 1 and 0.

How to get AMG's real numbers: a three-step plan
1
Ask the Registrar for what already exists. These columns come from records AMG keeps today and cover the arrows into NCLEX, employment, retention, and completion: academic (ATI level or GPA), remediation_done, review_session, record_error, retained, completed, nclex_pass, employed_6mo, plus ati_pop from AMG's ATI Predictive Analytics export. Ask for the last two or three graduating classes, about 300 or more students.
2
Protect students before the file leaves the Registrar. Replace real IDs with random study codes and keep the key with the Registrar; leave out names, birth dates, and contact details; share only the columns listed; and suppress any group smaller than 10. Keep the work within FERPA's legitimate-educational-interest use, and get IRB approval first if results may be published.
3
Link surveys later, with consent. teaching, clinical, support, resources, engagement, communication, and grad_sat need survey answers tied to study codes. Today's surveys are anonymous, so this means adding a consented, coded option to future surveys. faculty is set per course section.

Step 1, with each student's ATI predicted probability of passing from the ATI export, puts real β and p-values on 12 of the 32 arrows, including every arrow into NCLEX, employment, and completion. The request is on the schedule under "What's scheduled."

For statisticians: model specification (R, lavaan) 

        
Categorical outcomes (retention, completion, NCLEX pass) call for the WLSMV estimator with those variables declared as ordered. Faculty variables sit at the course-section level, so a full treatment needs multilevel SEM or cluster-robust standard errors. Survey indicators need student-level linkage, which the current anonymous surveys do not allow; a consented, ID-linked survey would be needed.

      

    


    
Technical note for statisticians: OLS with t-distribution intervals; Beta-Binomial conjugate posteriors, fall 2025 n=61 and spring 2026 n=49–50, counts reconstructed from reported percentages and treated as independent samples; Monte Carlo with Beta-distributed base rate, normal intervention and volatility terms, and binomial test outcomes. All computation runs in the browser from the figures on this page.

  






  

    
The sound of quality: AMG as a soundscape

    
Listening can reveal patterns a chart hides: several measures moving at once, small gaps, and how solid the evidence is. This section turns AMG's quality data into sound, organized by the six QSEN competencies that define quality and safety in pre-licensure nursing education. Each competency plays in its own pitch band, and the spectrogram draws the sound as it plays. Data as of September 30, 2026.


    

      

        

          

            
            
            
            
            
          

        

        

          
Program

          
        

        
Press play. Sound starts only when you choose, and you can stop it at any time.

        

          
          

        

        
Spectrogram of the whole piece, computed from the exact sound you hear: time runs left to right, pitch bottom to top, brighter means louder. Each labeled band is one QSEN competency. During playback a white line sweeps across it.

        
The score: what you will hear

        
Every note planned for the piece, drawn the way the spectrogram should show it. Wavy lines wobble (below benchmark); fuzzy halos hiss (indirect evidence).

        

      

      

        

          
How to listen

          
    
            
  • Higher pitch within a band = stronger result. Each competency has its own band; the higher a note sits in its band, the better that measure.
    • 
            
  • Smooth, steady tone = at or above the 80% benchmark.
    • 
            
  • A "wah-wah" wobble = below benchmark. The faster the wobble, the bigger the gap.
    • 
            
  • A breathy hiss = weak evidence. Clear tones come from direct measures; hiss means AMG only has indirect ones.
    • 
            
  • A rising slide = improvement over time; a falling slide or melody = decline.
    • 
          

          
Reading the spectrogram

          
Clean, thin horizontal lines are clear, on-target measures. Lines that pulse or break up are wobbling (below benchmark). Smudged, blurry lines carry hiss (weak evidence). Lines that climb are improvements.

How AMG's measures map to the six QSEN competencies

      
QSEN defines the knowledge, skills, and attitudes nursing programs should build. AMG does not yet assess students directly against QSEN, so each competency is heard through the closest measures AMG has. The mapping is ours and is meant for discussion, not an official QSEN assessment. Select a row to hear that competency alone.

      

      
Competency summaries written in our own words from the QSEN Institute's pre-licensure competencies (qsen.org), based on Cronenwett et al., Nursing Outlook, 2007. Score = average of the measures shown, each scaled to 0–100 (5-point means × 20).

    

    

      

        
Download the soundscape and its data

        
Every file comes from the same rendered sound, so the video, audio, spectrogram, and data always match. Files follow the program selected above.

        

          
          
          
          
          
          
        

        
        

        

      

      

        
The algorithm, open for checking

        
The data-to-sound translation is a published, repeatable recipe. The same inputs always produce the same sound, because even the hiss comes from a fixed random seed.

        
    
          
  1. Band. Each QSEN competency gets its own pitch range, a musical fifth wide, stacked from Safety (lowest) to Informatics (highest).
    2. 
          
  2. Pitch. A score from 40 to 100 moves the note up to 7 semitones within its band, snapped to a major scale: f = base × 2^(step/12).
    3. 
          
  3. Wobble. Below 80%, a twin tone is added slightly off pitch so the sound pulses: beat = min(7, 0.3 × (80 − score)) pulses per second.
    4. 
          
  4. Hiss. Evidence strength sets narrow-band noise around the note: none for direct measures, light for partial, heavier for indirect.
    5. 
          
  5. Change. Measures surveyed in both fall 2025 and spring 2026 slide between their two pitches; NCLEX histories play as short melodies.
    6. 
          
  6. Render and analyze. The piece is rendered once, offline, at 22,050 samples per second, then a Fourier transform (4,096-point Hann window) draws the spectrogram from that same audio.
    7.

    What could the scheduled actions do for AMG's results?
    
    
    A computer simulation of AMG's next three years, run 4,000 times. Each run plays out 2026 to 2028 twice: once with only the ups and downs of a normal year, and once with the scheduled actions added. Comparing the two shows what the actions could plausibly add. Nobody yet knows exactly how well each action will work, so the simulation draws each one's effect from a range and shows the full spread of results.
    

    
    
      
    
        
    Scheduled actions
    
        
    Every item in "What's scheduled" above is included here automatically, and anything added there appears here too. Items that measure or prepare rather than change results directly are modeled with no direct effect, so switching them off changes nothing. Switch any item off to see the results without it.
    
        
    
      
    
      
    
        
    
          
    
            
    100% means every eligible student gets each action as designed.

      Assumptions behind the simulation
      
    Effects are written as the share of students who would otherwise fall short that each action is assumed to help. For example, "cuts NCLEX-RN failures by 15%" means if 29 of 100 students would fail, about 4 fewer do. Each run draws an effect between the low and high values shown, most often near the typical value. These are planning assumptions for discussion, not measured results for AMG; they should be revised as real data arrives.
    
      
    
      
    Technical note: 4,000 Monte Carlo runs with common random numbers across scenarios. Baseline true rate drawn from Beta(k+1, n−k+1) around the 2025 value; yearly shocks N(0, σ) with σ = 6 points for NCLEX, 2 for completion, 5 for satisfaction; observed rates via normal approximation to the binomial. Action effects are triangular(min, mode, max) proportional reductions in the shortfall, multiplied by implementation level, effect-size setting, and a ramp-up schedule, then combined multiplicatively. "Partly recover" moves the baseline one-third of the remaining way each year toward the earlier average (RN 2023–2024, 90.2%; PN 2022–2024, 91.5%; NCLEX only). Cohort sizes: RN 183, PN 80, survey 50.
    
    
    
  
    

    


    
  
    
    
    Does AMG support the UN Sustainable Development Goals?
    
    
    A nursing school's biggest contributions to sustainable development are a skilled health workforce and quality, inclusive education. This section traces AMG's own evidence to the specific UN targets it can affect, and rates each link with the same five progress levels the UN's Sustainable Development Goals Report 2026 uses for the world.

    Evidence heatmap: AMG measures × UN targets
    
      
    Each row is an area AMG measures; each column is a UN target it can affect. Color shows progress, using the UN report's five levels. Big squares are direct contributions; small squares are supporting ones; striped squares are links AMG doesn't measure yet.
    
      
    Select any square to see the story behind that link: AMG's result, why it earned its color, and what would move it up. A good place to start is the red square in the top row, where the NCLEX-RN decline meets the health workforce target (3.c).
    
      
    
        
    
        
    
      
    
      
    
      
    What each target number means
    
      
    UN targets are numbered by Goal: 4.3 is the third target under Goal 4, and a letter (such as 3.c) marks a target about how the Goal is achieved.
    
      
    
    
    

    
    
      
    
      
    
        
    Measured against the UN's yardstick
    
        
    Share of links in each progress level. The world's figures cover 139 global targets with trend data; AMG's cover its measured links. The units differ, so read this as a way to frame AMG's position, not a direct comparison.
    
        
    
      
    
    
    
    
    
      How the ratings are decided
      
    Each AMG measure is compared with the 80% benchmark used across this platform (a 4.00 of 5 rating counts as 80%), or with the program's own SPOE target where one exists (RN completion 75%, LPN completion 70%). On track: at or above 80% and not falling. Moderate progress: at or above 80% but falling, within 5 points of 80%, or up at least 10 points from the earlier reading. Regression: below 80% and down at least 5 points. Stagnation: below 80% and staying within 2 points across several readings. Marginal progress: any other result below 80%, including a single reading. Not measured: a link that matters but has no AMG data yet.
    
      
    SDG targets are written for countries, so AMG's role is local and partial: it adds to national progress rather than achieving any target by itself. The mapping of AMG measures to targets is our interpretation, offered for discussion. Target summaries are in plain language; see the UN's official wording at unstats.un.org/sdgs. World figures are from The Sustainable Development Goals Report 2026. SDG names are used for reference; the official SDG icons and colors are not reproduced.
